library(nlmixr2lib)

# Model and source

* Citation: Kumar M, Lanke S, Yadav A, Ette M, Mager DE, Shah DK.
  Inter-Antibody Variability in the Clinical Pharmacokinetics of Monoclonal
  Antibodies Characterized Using Population Physiologically Based
  Pharmacokinetic Modeling. Antibodies. 2024;13(3):54.
  doi:10.3390/antib13030054
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/antib13030054>
* Upstream framework: Shah DK, Betts AM. J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn.
  2012;39(1):67-86. doi:10.1007/s10928-011-9232-2

Kumar 2024 takes the Shah & Betts 2012 platform PBPK model (packaged
separately as `Shah_2012_mAb_PBPK`) and turns it into a *population* model
in which the "individuals" are **antibodies rather than patients**. Mean
clinical plasma profiles were digitised for 143 mAbs; 55 showed linear PK;
44 with IV data built the IV model and the 16 that also had SC data built
the SC model. Two of the four Shah & Betts system parameters (`CLup`,
`kdeg`) were re-estimated with inter-antibody random effects, and two new
absorption parameters (`kSC`, `S_LU`) were introduced for the SC route.

Two model files come out of this one paper, matching the two models the
authors built:

| File | Route | States | Estimated parameters |
|------|-------|--------|----------------------|
| `Kumar_2024_mAb_popPBPK_iv` | IV | 93 | `CLup`, `kdeg` (+ 2 etas) |
| `Kumar_2024_mAb_popPBPK_sc` | SC | 99 | `CLup`, `kdeg`, `kSC`, `S_LU` (+ 4 etas) |

```{r load-models}
mod_iv <- rxode2(readModelDb("Kumar_2024_mAb_popPBPK_iv"))
mod_sc <- rxode2(readModelDb("Kumar_2024_mAb_popPBPK_sc"))

c(iv_states = length(mod_iv$state), sc_states = length(mod_sc$state))
```

# Population

The 44 IV antibodies and 16 SC antibodies are drawn overwhelmingly from
published phase 1 single-dose and dose-escalation studies, in healthy
volunteers and in patients (oncology, rheumatoid arthritis, asthma,
psoriasis, infectious disease). Kumar 2024 Supplementary Table S3 lists
per-antibody approval status, phase, country, and year.

Two deliberate exclusions define the model's scope:

* Antibodies with **dose-dependent (target-mediated) disposition** were
  removed by dose-normalising the digitised profiles, so the model describes
  **linear mAb disposition only** and carries no TMDD terms.
* **Panobacumab** (an IgM) and **suvratoxumab** (Fc-modified) were dropped
  despite showing linear PK, because their FcRn affinity differs
  substantially from the rest of the IgG set.

The underlying human physiology is the Shah & Betts 2012 Table 4
**71 kg male** reference; there are no subject-level covariates in the
model at all.

```{r population}
str(mod_iv$meta$population)
```

# Source trace

Every value in both `ini()` blocks, and each structural choice, traced to
its source location.

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|----------|-------|--------|
| `CLup` (pinocytosis per unit endosomal volume) | 0.32 L/h/L (RSE 5.6%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2; abstract |
| `omega_CLup` | 73% (RSE 3.2%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2 |
| `kdeg` (endosomal degradation, FcRn-unbound) | 26.1 1/h (RSE 11%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2; abstract |
| `omega_kdeg` | 46% (RSE 17.6%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2 |
| `kSC` (local degradation at injection site) | 0.0015 1/h (RSE 66%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2; abstract |
| `omega_kSC` | 193% (RSE 24.7%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2 |
| `S_LU` (lymphatic-uptake scaling) | 0.54 (RSE 14%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2; abstract |
| `omega_S_LU` | 49% (RSE 21.1%) | Kumar 2024 Suppl. Table S2 |
| Central plasma volume | 1412 mL | Kumar 2024 Section 2.5 |
| Central blood-cell volume | 1155 mL | Kumar 2024 Section 2.5 |
| Skin sub-volumes and flows (SC model) | Table 1 col. "Skin (SC)" | Kumar 2024 Table 1 |
| Subcutaneous sub-volumes and flows | Table 1 col. "SC (SC)" | Kumar 2024 Table 1 |
| All other organ volumes and flows (human, 71 kg) | Table 4 | Shah & Betts 2012 Table 4 |
| Vascular reflection coefficients `sigma_V` | 0.95 / 0.90 / 0.85, brain 0.99 | Shah & Betts 2012 "Model parameters" |
| Lymphatic reflection coefficient `sigma_IS` | 0.2 (all tissues) | Shah & Betts 2012 "Model parameters" |
| Lymph flow | plasma flow / 500 | Shah & Betts 2012 "Model parameters" |
| Endosomal FcRn concentration | 4.98e-5 M | Shah & Betts 2012 Table 6 |
| `FR` (recycled fraction) | 0.715 | Shah & Betts 2012 "Model parameters" |
| `kon` / `koff` (human) | 5.59e8 1/M/h, 23.9 1/h | Shah & Betts 2012 "Model parameters" |
| Lymph-node return flow | 3.670 L/h | Shah & Betts 2012 Table 4 row "Ly. Node" |
| Blood / blood-cell / lymph-node ODEs, tissue ODEs | Eqs 1-3, 4-10, liver 11-12 | Shah & Betts 2012 |
| SC interstitium ODE (adds `S_LU`, `kSC`) | Section 2.4 | Kumar 2024 |

Note the provenance split: Kumar 2024 states in Section 2.5 that "all model
parameters apart from pinocytosis rate (CLup) and non-specific degradation
rate of unbound antibody (kdeg) are the same as those used for humans by
Shah and Betts", so the physiology rows above are read from the upstream
paper, which was available when this model was built.

## Units in the ODE system

| Quantity | Units |
|----------|-------|
| State amounts (`vp_*`, `bc_*`, `eu_*`, `eb_*`, `is_*`) | nmol |
| State amounts (free FcRn, `fr_*`) | nmol (1:1 with mAb) |
| Concentrations (state / volume) | nmol/L (= nM) |
| Time | h |
| Volumes | L |
| Flows | L/h |
| `kon` | 1/(M h), converted internally to 1/(nM h) |
| `koff`, `kdeg`, `kSC` | 1/h |
| `CLup` | L/h per L of endosomal volume |
| `S_LU` | unitless |

Doses are supplied in nmol: `dose_nmol = dose_mg / MW_g_per_mol * 1e6`.
IV doses go to `plasma`; **SC doses go to `is_subcutaneous`** (the
interstitial space of the injection-site compartment), not to a `depot`.

```{r dose-helper}
mw_igg <- 145000  # g/mol, typical IgG1
mg_to_nmol <- function(mg) mg / mw_igg * 1e6
```

# Three source reconciliations

The paper inherits its structure by reference rather than printing it, so
three points had to be resolved against the upstream sources. Each is
recorded here because each changes the numbers.

## 1. `CLup` scales by *each tissue's* endosomal volume

Shah & Betts 2012 define `CLup` as the "rate of pinocytosis per unit
endosomal space", and their text says it is multiplied by the endosomal
volume of the given tissue. Their ADAPT 5 code, however, gives every
tissue the same uptake clearance, `CLup * V_endosomal,TOTAL`, and their
Table 6 estimate (0.0366 L/h/L) was made with that form (see the
`Shah_2012_mAb_PBPK` vignette). Kumar 2024 does not say which form it
uses. The per-tissue form is used here, because the same laboratory's
later implementation uses it and Kumar 2024's estimate is on its scale:

1. Chang 2019 ("augmenting our previously published platform PBPK
   model") prints `CLup_i = CLup * V_ES_i` and sets `CLup` to 0.55 L/h/L
   for all tissues except the brain. That is 15 x 0.0366: over the 2012
   model's 15 tissues, the per-tissue form with 0.55 L/h/L gives the same
   total pinocytosis clearance as the 2012 code's form with 0.0366 L/h/L.
2. Kumar 2024's estimate, 0.32 L/h/L (Suppl. Table S2), is of the same
   order as Chang 2019's per-tissue value, and about 9 times the 0.0366
   L/h/L of the whole-body form.

## 2. The brain compartment is in the model

Kumar 2024 Section 2.2 enumerates "fifteen tissues" and omits the brain.
That enumeration is wrong: Figure 1 of the same paper draws a Brain box,
and the paper's own arithmetic requires it. Section 2.5 derives the central
plasma volume as total blood plasma minus the vascular volume held in the
tissues. Using Shah & Betts Table 4:

```{r brain-arithmetic}
tissue_plasma <- c(heart = 13.1, lung = 55.0, muscle = 662, skin = 127,
                   adipose = 148, bone = 224, kidney = 18.2, liver = 183,
                   small_intestine = 6.15, large_intestine = 8.74,
                   pancreas = 5.70, thymus = 0.353, spleen = 26.8,
                   other = 204)
brain_plasma <- 31.9
total_plasma <- 3126

data.frame(
  scenario = c("without brain", "with brain", "Kumar 2024 Section 2.5"),
  central_plasma_mL = round(c(total_plasma - sum(tissue_plasma),
                              total_plasma - sum(tissue_plasma) - brain_plasma,
                              1412), 1)
)
```

Subtracting the brain's vascular plasma reproduces the paper's stated
1412 mL exactly; omitting it gives 1444 mL. The same holds for blood cells
(2558 - 1374.7 - 26.1 = 1157 mL vs the paper's 1155 mL). The brain is
therefore retained.

## 3. `S_LU` is applied to both ends of the SC-to-lymph flux

Kumar's SC interstitium equation multiplies the convective efflux by
`S_LU`, but the lymph-node equation printed just above it sums the
unscaled `(1 - sigma_IS) * L_SC * C_SC` term. Taken literally that creates
mass: with `S_LU` = 0.54 the lymph node would gain almost twice what the SC
compartment loses. `S_LU` is applied to both terms here.

The paper's own sensitivity analysis confirms this. Under the literal
reading, raising `S_LU` would drain the SC site faster while the lymph node
gains only in proportion to the (now lower) SC concentration, so exposure
would *fall*. Figure 7 shows exposure *rising* with `S_LU`, which only the
mass-balanced form produces.

# Mass-balance check

With `kSC` and `kdeg` switched off, both models are closed systems and
total mAb mass must be conserved. This catches structural ODE errors that
numerical agreement alone would hide.

```{r mass-balance}
organs <- c("heart", "lung", "muscle", "skin", "adipose", "bone", "brain",
            "kidney", "liver", "small_intestine", "large_intestine",
            "pancreas", "thymus", "spleen", "other")
organs_sc <- c(organs, "subcutaneous")

mab_cols <- function(org) {
  c("plasma", "bcc", "lnode",
    paste0("vp_", org), paste0("bc_", org),
    paste0("eu_", org), paste0("eb_", org), paste0("is_", org))
}

dose_nmol <- mg_to_nmol(5 * 71)   # 5 mg/kg in a 71 kg adult

closed_iv <- mod_iv |> ini(lkdeg = log(1e-12))
ev_iv <- et(amt = dose_nmol, cmt = "plasma", time = 0) |> et(seq(0, 336, by = 8))
sim_closed_iv <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(zeroRe(closed_iv), ev_iv))
tot_iv <- rowSums(sim_closed_iv[, mab_cols(organs), drop = FALSE])

closed_sc <- mod_sc |> ini(lkdeg = log(1e-12), lksc = log(1e-12))
ev_sc <- et(amt = dose_nmol, cmt = "is_subcutaneous", time = 0) |>
  et(seq(0, 336, by = 8))
sim_closed_sc <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(zeroRe(closed_sc), ev_sc))
tot_sc <- rowSums(sim_closed_sc[, mab_cols(organs_sc), drop = FALSE])

data.frame(
  model = c("IV (93 states)", "SC (99 states)"),
  dose_nmol = round(dose_nmol, 1),
  total_at_t0 = round(c(tot_iv[1], tot_sc[1]), 1),
  total_at_14d = round(c(tail(tot_iv, 1), tail(tot_sc, 1)), 1),
  max_rel_error = signif(c(max(abs(tot_iv / dose_nmol - 1)),
                           max(abs(tot_sc / dose_nmol - 1))), 3)
)
```

Free plus bound FcRn is also conserved per tissue, since the FcRn ODE is
the exact negative of the bound-complex formation and release terms.

```{r fcrn-conservation}
fcrn_M <- 4.98e-5
v_e <- c(heart = 0.00171, muscle = 0.150, liver = 0.0107)
chk <- sapply(names(v_e), function(o) {
  tot <- sim_closed_iv[[paste0("fr_", o)]] + sim_closed_iv[[paste0("eb_", o)]]
  max(abs(tot / (fcrn_M * 1e9 * v_e[[o]]) - 1))
})
signif(chk, 3)
```

# Typical-value profiles

A 5 mg/kg dose in the 71 kg reference adult, by each route. The etas are
zeroed so these are the population-typical antibody.

```{r typical-profiles}
tgrid <- c(seq(0, 48, by = 2), seq(60, 24 * 84, by = 12))

sim_iv <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(
  zeroRe(mod_iv),
  et(amt = dose_nmol, cmt = "plasma", time = 0) |> et(tgrid)
))
sim_sc <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(
  zeroRe(mod_sc),
  et(amt = dose_nmol, cmt = "is_subcutaneous", time = 0) |> et(tgrid)
))

typical <- bind_rows(
  sim_iv |> transmute(time, Cc, route = "IV"),
  sim_sc |> transmute(time, Cc, route = "SC")
)
```

```{r fig-typical, fig.cap = "Typical-value plasma profiles for a linear mAb after 5 mg/kg IV and SC, from the Kumar 2024 popPBPK model."}
# The time-zero rows, kept for PKNCA, are left off the log axis.
typical |>
  filter(time != 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(time / 24, Cc, colour = route)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Time (days)", y = "Plasma mAb (nM)", colour = "Route",
       title = "Typical-value linear-mAb PK, 5 mg/kg")
```

The SC curve shows the slow, flat absorption characteristic of lymphatic
uptake, peaking around a week.

# PKNCA validation

```{r pknca}
# `route` and `dose` are reserved PKNCA column names and must not be used as
# grouping variables; the arm label is carried as `treatment` and the dose
# amount as `amt`. `route` is kept for its intended PKNCA purpose.
nca_conc <- typical |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  mutate(treatment = route, id = ifelse(route == "IV", 1L, 2L)) |>
  select(id, treatment, time, Cc)

# Both arms must carry a time-zero record, or PKNCA warns that the AUC
# interval starts before the first measurement. The simulation grid begins
# at 0, so this is an assertion rather than a repair.
stopifnot(all(table(nca_conc$treatment[nca_conc$time == 0]) == 1))

nca_dose <- data.frame(
  id = c(1L, 2L),
  treatment = c("IV", "SC"),
  time = 0,
  amt = dose_nmol,
  route = c("intravascular", "extravascular")
)

o_conc <- PKNCAconc(nca_conc, Cc ~ time | treatment + id,
                    concu = "nmol/L", timeu = "h")
o_dose <- PKNCAdose(nca_dose, amt ~ time | treatment + id,
                    route = "route", doseu = "nmol")

intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf,
  cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  half.life = TRUE, cl.obs = TRUE
)

res <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = intervals))
nca_tab <- as.data.frame(res)
```

```{r pknca-table}
nca_wide <- nca_tab |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "aucinf.obs",
                         "half.life", "cl.obs")) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)

nca_disp <- nca_wide |>
  transmute(
    treatment,
    `Cmax (nM)`        = signif(cmax, 4),
    `Tmax (days)`      = signif(tmax / 24, 3),
    `AUClast (nM*h)`   = signif(auclast, 4),
    `AUCinf (nM*h)`    = signif(aucinf.obs, 4),
    `t1/2 (days)`      = signif(half.life / 24, 3),
    `CL/F (L/day)`     = signif(cl.obs * 24, 3)
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(Route = treatment)

knitr::kable(nca_disp,
             caption = "PKNCA parameters from the typical-value profiles.")
```

## Comparison against published values

Kumar 2024 does not tabulate NCA parameters, so the simulated values are
checked against the quantities the paper and the mAb literature do pin
down.

```{r nca-check}
f_sc <- nca_wide$aucinf.obs[nca_wide$treatment == "SC"] /
  nca_wide$aucinf.obs[nca_wide$treatment == "IV"]
thalf <- nca_wide$half.life[nca_wide$treatment == "IV"] / 24
cl_iv <- nca_wide$cl.obs[nca_wide$treatment == "IV"] * 24
tmax_sc <- nca_wide$tmax[nca_wide$treatment == "SC"] / 24

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("IV terminal half-life (days)",
                 "IV clearance (L/day)",
                 "SC bioavailability (AUC ratio)",
                 "SC Tmax (days)"),
    Simulated = signif(c(thalf, cl_iv, f_sc, tmax_sc), 3),
    Expected = c("~2-3 weeks for a linear IgG1",
                 "~0.2-0.3 for a linear IgG1",
                 "~0.5-0.8 typical mAb SC",
                 "~4-8 typical mAb SC")
  ),
  caption = "Simulated summary PK against canonical linear-mAb behaviour."
)
```

The clearance is an *emergent* quantity: nothing in the model is a
clearance term, so it falls out of `CLup`, `kdeg`, `FR`, the FcRn binding
constants and the whole-body physiology together. Recovering ~0.2 L/day
shows that the re-estimated `CLup` and `kdeg`, in the per-tissue form, give
the clearance of a linear IgG1.

# Replicating Figure 7 (local sensitivity analysis)

Figure 7 reports the percent change in SC AUC when `kSC` and `S_LU` are
each altered by +/-50%, using
`% change = (AUC_{+/-50%} - AUC_orig) / AUC_orig` with all other
parameters at their population values (Kumar 2024 Section 2.6). This is the
paper's only quantitative, digit-level result for the SC layer, so it is
the primary validation target.

```{r fig7-replication}
auc_sc_for <- function(ksc_mult = 1, slu_mult = 1) {
  p <- c(lksc = log(0.0015 * ksc_mult), lslu = log(0.54 * slu_mult))
  s <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(
    zeroRe(mod_sc),
    et(amt = dose_nmol, cmt = "is_subcutaneous", time = 0) |> et(tgrid),
    params = p
  ))
  sum(diff(s$time) * (head(s$Cc, -1) + tail(s$Cc, -1)) / 2)
}

auc_base <- auc_sc_for()
pct <- function(x) (x / auc_base - 1) * 100

fig7 <- data.frame(
  Scenario = c("kSC -50%", "kSC +50%", "S_LU -50%", "S_LU +50%"),
  Simulated = round(c(pct(auc_sc_for(ksc_mult = 0.5)),
                      pct(auc_sc_for(ksc_mult = 1.5)),
                      pct(auc_sc_for(slu_mult = 0.5)),
                      pct(auc_sc_for(slu_mult = 1.5))), 1),
  Published = c(5.4, -4.9, -15.8, 8.6)
)
fig7$Difference <- round(fig7$Simulated - fig7$Published, 1)

knitr::kable(
  fig7 |> dplyr::rename(`% change in AUC (simulated)` = Simulated,
                        `% change in AUC (Kumar Fig 7)` = Published,
                        `Difference (pp)` = Difference),
  caption = "Replicates Kumar 2024 Figure 7."
)
```

```{r fig-7, fig.cap = "Replicates Kumar 2024 Figure 7: local sensitivity of SC AUC to kSC and S_LU."}
fig7 |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Simulated, Published),
                      names_to = "source", values_to = "pct") |>
  ggplot(aes(Scenario, pct, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% change in AUC", fill = NULL,
       title = "Local sensitivity analysis of the SC absorption parameters")
```

**The `kSC` arm reproduces exactly** (+5.4% and -4.9%, matching the
published values to the printed precision). That agreement validates the
`kSC` value, the SC interstitial volume, the AUC window, and the
percent-change definition all at once.

The `S_LU` arm has the correct sign, the correct rank ordering (`S_LU` is
the more sensitive parameter, as the paper concludes) and the correct
asymmetry, but is about 1.5x too large. Inverting the published
percentages through the competition between lymphatic escape and local
loss implies the authors' SC bioavailability was roughly 0.76-0.81, where
this implementation gives:

```{r implied-f}
signif(f_sc, 3)
```

Both lie inside the observed mAb range, and no parameter has been adjusted
to close the gap. See Errata for the candidate explanations.

# Monte Carlo comparison with Supplementary Figure S1 (IV)

Kumar 2024 Supplementary Figure S1 simulates the IV model after 1 mg/kg:
the median of the simulated antibodies and a 90% band (5th to 95th
percentile), drawn over observed profiles dose-normalized to 1 mg/kg and a
curve from the Shah & Betts 2012 model. The median and the edges of the
band were read from the published figure. On a log axis a reading has
about the same relative precision anywhere on the axis, roughly +/-5% where
a line is clear; readings of dashed lines, and of lines crowded by
observations, are less certain.

Because the random effects are **inter-antibody**, each draw is a
different hypothetical antibody, not a different patient. The medians and
percentiles in this section and the next come from one Monte Carlo cohort
of 200 antibodies (the paper used 1000). Its etas are drawn in R from the
model's omega matrix (seed 20240709) and passed to the typical-value model
as parameters, so the cohort is the same on every machine and with every
rxode2 version. A percentile of 200 antibodies still moves from one cohort
to another, so each check below has a tolerance wide enough for that.

```{r mc-cohort}
n_ab <- 200
# Rows of independent standard normals times the upper Cholesky factor have
# covariance omega.
set.seed(20240709)
eta_mc <- matrix(rnorm(n_ab * ncol(mod_sc$omega)), n_ab) %*% chol(mod_sc$omega)
colnames(eta_mc) <- colnames(mod_sc$omega)
cohort <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n_ab), eta_mc)
# The IV model's two random effects are the first two of the SC model's.
stopifnot(identical(
  diag(mod_iv$omega),
  diag(mod_sc$omega)[names(diag(mod_iv$omega))]
))

nm_to_ugml <- function(nm) nm * mw_igg / 1e6

# Solves one row of `eta` per id with the typical-value model and keeps only
# Cc: the full output of the 93- and 99-state models has about 280 columns
# per row, so large sets are solved in chunks.
sim_cohort <- function(model, amt, cmt, times, eta, chunk = 500) {
  starts <- seq(1, nrow(eta), by = chunk)
  out <- lapply(starts, function(i) {
    p <- eta[i:min(i + chunk - 1, nrow(eta)), , drop = FALSE]
    ev <- et(amt = amt, cmt = cmt, time = 0) |> et(times) |> et(id = p$id)
    s <- rxSolve(model, ev, params = p, returnType = "data.frame")
    data.frame(id = s$id, time = s$time, Cc = s$Cc)
  })
  bind_rows(out)
}

# Median and 5th/95th percentiles across the cohort, in ug/mL. The output
# times start after the dose, so every row is a post-dose concentration.
cohort_stats <- function(sim) {
  sim |>
    mutate(conc = nm_to_ugml(Cc)) |>
    group_by(time) |>
    summarise(
      median = median(conc),
      p05 = unname(quantile(conc, 0.05)),
      p95 = unname(quantile(conc, 0.95)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

typ_iv <- zeroRe(mod_iv)
typ_sc <- zeroRe(mod_sc)
```

```{r figS1-published}
# Kumar 2024 Supplementary Figure S1, 1 mg/kg IV: median, 95th and 5th
# percentile of the simulated antibodies (ug/mL), read from the figure.
s1_median <- data.frame(
  time = c(42, 60, 84, 105, 130, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400, 450, 500, 550,
           600, 650, 690),
  published = c(13.9, 12.6, 11.4, 10.6, 9.80, 9.27, 8.22, 7.36, 6.65, 5.44,
                4.97, 4.52, 4.13, 3.79, 3.46, 3.22)
)
s1_p95 <- data.frame(
  time = c(250, 500, 600, 700),
  published = c(10.9, 8.39, 7.74, 7.17)
)
s1_p05 <- data.frame(
  time = c(200, 300, 336, 400, 500, 600, 700),
  published = c(4.61, 3.00, 2.58, 2.00, 1.33, 0.876, 0.595)
)
```

The whole-body form of the pinocytosis clearance, which the Shah & Betts
ADAPT code uses (reconciliation 1), gives every tissue the clearance
`CLup` times the sum of the 15 tissue endosomal volumes. It is built here
from the packaged model's own volumes, so the two forms differ only in that
term.

```{r figS1-wholebody}
iv_lhs <- vapply(mod_iv$lstExpr, function(e) {
  if (is.call(e) && identical(e[[1]], as.name("<-"))) deparse(e[[2]]) else ""
}, character(1))
v_e <- vapply(mod_iv$lstExpr[grepl("^v_[a-z]{2}_e$", iv_lhs)],
              function(e) eval(e[[3]]), numeric(1))
clu_names <- grep("^clu_[a-z]{2}$", iv_lhs, value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(v_e) == 15, length(clu_names) == 15)
clu_wb <- lapply(clu_names, function(nm) {
  str2lang(sprintf("%s <- clup_pv * %.10g", nm, sum(v_e)))
})
mod_iv_wb <- suppressMessages(
  eval(as.call(c(list(quote(rxode2::model), quote(mod_iv)), clu_wb)))
)
```

```{r figS1-sim}
s1_times <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 6, seq(12, 720, by = 12), s1_median$time,
                          s1_p95$time, s1_p05$time)))
dose_s1 <- mg_to_nmol(71)  # 1 mg/kg in the 71 kg reference adult
iv_eta <- cohort[, c("id", "etalclup", "etalkdeg")]
st_s1 <- cohort_stats(sim_cohort(typ_iv, dose_s1, "plasma", s1_times, iv_eta))
st_s1_wb <- cohort_stats(
  sim_cohort(zeroRe(mod_iv_wb), dose_s1, "plasma", s1_times, iv_eta)
)

s1_cmp <- s1_median |>
  left_join(st_s1 |> select(time, simulated = median), by = "time") |>
  left_join(st_s1_wb |> select(time, whole_body = median), by = "time") |>
  mutate(ratio = simulated / published, ratio_wb = whole_body / published)
s1_hi <- s1_p95 |>
  left_join(st_s1 |> select(time, simulated = p95), by = "time") |>
  mutate(ratio = simulated / published)
s1_lo <- s1_p05 |>
  left_join(st_s1 |> select(time, simulated = p05), by = "time") |>
  mutate(ratio = simulated / published)

s1_early <- s1_cmp$time <= 150
s1_ratio_at <- function(t) s1_cmp$ratio[s1_cmp$time == t]
s1_wb_below <- 1 - s1_cmp$ratio_wb[s1_early]
# Half-life over 300-690 h, from a log-linear fit to a median curve.
s1_late <- s1_cmp$time >= 300
s1_thalf <- function(conc) {
  -log(2) / coef(lm(log(conc[s1_late]) ~ s1_cmp$time[s1_late]))[[2]] / 24
}

knitr::kable(
  s1_cmp |>
    transmute(
      `Time (h)` = time,
      `Published median` = published,
      `Simulated median` = signif(simulated, 3),
      `Ratio` = round(ratio, 2),
      `Whole-body form median` = signif(whole_body, 3),
      `Ratio (whole-body)` = round(ratio_wb, 2)
    ),
  caption = paste("Supplementary Figure S1 median (ug/mL) after 1 mg/kg IV",
                  "against the median of", n_ab, "simulated antibodies.")
)

knitr::kable(
  bind_rows(
    s1_hi |> mutate(Percentile = "95th"),
    s1_lo |> mutate(Percentile = "5th")
  ) |>
    transmute(Percentile, `Time (h)` = time, Published = published,
              Simulated = signif(simulated, 3), Ratio = round(ratio, 2)),
  caption = "Supplementary Figure S1 band edges (ug/mL) against the simulated percentiles."
)

stopifnot(
  # Distribution phase: the simulated median follows the published one.
  all(abs(s1_cmp$ratio[s1_early] - 1) < 0.1),
  # Later the model is above the published median: at every time from
  # 300 h, by more than 10% in the middle of 400-690 h, and by 10-50% at
  # 690 h.
  all(s1_cmp$ratio[s1_late] > 1.03),
  median(s1_cmp$ratio[s1_cmp$time >= 400]) > 1.1,
  s1_ratio_at(690) > 1.1, s1_ratio_at(690) < 1.5,
  # So its half-life over 300-690 h is more than a day longer.
  s1_thalf(s1_cmp$simulated) - s1_thalf(s1_cmp$published) > 1,
  # The whole-body form is 12-40% below the published median at every time
  # over 42-150 h.
  all(s1_wb_below > 0.12), all(s1_wb_below < 0.4),
  # The 95th percentiles agree; the published 5th percentile is lower.
  all(abs(s1_hi$ratio - 1) < 0.15),
  all(s1_lo$ratio[s1_lo$time >= 300] > 1.2)
)
```

```{r fig-S1, fig.cap = "Replicates Kumar 2024 Supplementary Figure S1: 1 mg/kg IV. Line and band are the median and 5th-95th percentiles of 200 simulated antibodies; points are read from the published median (filled) and band edges (open)."}

  s1_median |> mutate(stat = "Median"),
  s1_p95 |> mutate(stat = "5th or 95th percentile"),

  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = s1_pub, aes(y = published, shape = stat), size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Median = 16, `5th or 95th percentile` = 1)) +

Over 42-150 h, the distribution phase, the simulated median is within
`r round(100 * max(abs(s1_cmp$ratio[s1_early] - 1)), 1)`% of the published
one. From about 200 h the published median declines faster: the model is
`r round(100 * (s1_ratio_at(250) - 1))`% higher at 250 h,
`r round(100 * (s1_ratio_at(500) - 1))`% higher at 500 h and
`r round(100 * (s1_ratio_at(690) - 1))`% higher at 690 h. Over 300-690 h the
published median has a half-life of
`r round(s1_thalf(s1_cmp$published), 1)` days and the simulated one
`r round(s1_thalf(s1_cmp$simulated), 1)` days. The 95th percentiles agree
within `r round(100 * max(abs(s1_hi$ratio - 1)), 1)`%, while the published
5th percentile is lower than the simulated one, by a factor of
`r round(s1_lo$ratio[s1_lo$time == 700], 1)` at 700 h, so the published
cohort has more quickly cleared antibodies. The cause was not determined;
it is recorded under Assumptions and deviations.

The form of the pinocytosis clearance does not explain the difference. With
the whole-body form (`CLup` times `r round(1000 * sum(v_e), 1)` mL of
endosomal volume in every tissue) the simulated median is
`r round(100 * min(s1_wb_below))`-`r round(100 * max(s1_wb_below))`% below
the published one over 42-150 h, where the packaged model matches it.

# Monte Carlo prediction window (Figure 8)

Kumar 2024 used the SC model to predict a window for SC mAb PK a priori,
and overlaid nine antibodies that were not used to build the model
(Figure 8). Each panel is one antibody at its highest dose, from 70 to
900 mg, with a solid line and a dashed 5th-95th percentile band from 1000
simulated antibodies. The caption does not say which statistic the solid
line is. The solid line of every panel, and the band of the three 600 mg
panels, were read from the published figure.

The solid line is compared with the mean over the population of
antibodies, which is computed here without sampling. The concentration is
integrated over the normal distribution of the four random effects by
Gauss-Hermite quadrature: a tensor-product grid of nodes, mapped through
the Cholesky factor of omega, where each node is one typical-value solve
and carries the product of the one-dimensional weights. The median and the
band come from the 200-antibody cohort above.

```{r quadrature}
# Gauss-Hermite nodes and weights for E[f(Z)], Z ~ N(0, 1): the eigenvalues
# of the Jacobi matrix of the probabilists' Hermite polynomials, and the
# squared first components of its eigenvectors (Golub-Welsch).
gh_nodes <- function(n) {
  if (n == 1) {
    return(list(z = 0, w = 1))
  }
  b <- sqrt(seq_len(n - 1))
  jac <- diag(0, n)
  jac[cbind(seq_len(n - 1), seq_len(n - 1) + 1)] <- b
  jac[cbind(seq_len(n - 1) + 1, seq_len(n - 1))] <- b
  e <- eigen(jac, symmetric = TRUE)
  list(z = e$values, w = e$vectors[1, ]^2)
}

# Tensor-product grid over the random effects, n[k] nodes for the k-th eta
# of omega; one row per node, with its eta values and weight.
gh_grid <- function(omega, n) {
  nodes <- lapply(n, gh_nodes)
  idx <- expand.grid(lapply(nodes, function(g) seq_along(g$z)))
  z <- vapply(seq_along(nodes), function(k) nodes[[k]]$z[idx[[k]]],
              numeric(nrow(idx)))
  w <- apply(vapply(seq_along(nodes), function(k) nodes[[k]]$w[idx[[k]]],
                    numeric(nrow(idx))), 1, prod)
  eta <- z %*% chol(omega)
  colnames(eta) <- colnames(omega)
  data.frame(id = seq_len(nrow(eta)), eta, w = w)
}

# Weighted sum over the nodes at each time, in ug/mL.
quad_mean <- function(sim, grid) {
  sim |>
    mutate(w = grid$w[match(id, grid$id)]) |>
    group_by(time) |>
    summarise(mean = sum(w * nm_to_ugml(Cc)), .groups = "drop")
}

quad_solve <- function(dose_mg, times, n) {
  grid <- gh_grid(mod_sc$omega, n)
  sim <- sim_cohort(typ_sc, mg_to_nmol(dose_mg), "is_subcutaneous", times,
                    grid[, setdiff(names(grid), "w")])
  quad_mean(sim, grid)
}

# More nodes on kdeg and kSC, whose spread drives the late concentrations.
fig8_nodes <- c(etalclup = 3, etalkdeg = 5, etalksc = 5, etalslu = 3)
stopifnot(identical(names(fig8_nodes), colnames(mod_sc$omega)))

# The rule integrates polynomials up to degree 2n - 1 exactly, so the grid
# reproduces the weights' total and the omega matrix.
g5 <- gh_nodes(5)
fig8_grid <- gh_grid(mod_sc$omega, fig8_nodes)
eta_cols <- colnames(mod_sc$omega)
stopifnot(
  abs(sum(g5$w) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(sum(g5$w * g5$z^4) - 3) < 1e-10,
  abs(sum(fig8_grid$w) - 1) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(crossprod(as.matrix(fig8_grid[eta_cols]) * sqrt(fig8_grid$w)) -
            mod_sc$omega)) < 1e-10
)
```

Before the comparison, the grid is checked: at the lowest and the highest
dose, adding two nodes on any one random effect must change the mean by
less than 1% at every time compared with the figure.

```{r fig8-convergence}
conv_doses <- range(fig8_panels$dose_mg)
fig8_conv <- bind_rows(lapply(conv_doses, function(d) {
  times <- sort(unique(fig8_pub$time[fig8_pub$dose_mg == d]))
  base <- quad_solve(d, times, fig8_nodes)
  bind_rows(lapply(names(fig8_nodes), function(k) {
    finer <- fig8_nodes
    finer[[k]] <- finer[[k]] + 2
    ref <- quad_solve(d, times, finer)
    data.frame(dose_mg = d, refined = k, nodes = prod(finer),
               max_rel_change = max(abs(base$mean / ref$mean - 1)))
  }))
}))

knitr::kable(
  fig8_conv |>
    transmute(`Dose (mg)` = dose_mg, `Random effect with 2 more nodes` = refined,
              Nodes = nodes,
              `Largest change of the mean (%)` = signif(100 * max_rel_change, 2)),
  caption = paste0("Convergence of the quadrature mean from the ",
                   prod(fig8_nodes), "-node grid (",
                   paste(fig8_nodes, collapse = " x "), ").")
)

stopifnot(all(fig8_conv$max_rel_change < 0.01))
```

```{r fig8-sim}
fig8_doses <- sort(unique(fig8_panels$dose_mg))
fig8_times <- function(d) {
  tmax <- max(fig8_panels$xmax[fig8_panels$dose_mg == d])

                seq(480, min(tmax, 3000), by = 120),

fig8_mc <- bind_rows(lapply(fig8_doses, function(d) {
  sim <- sim_cohort(typ_sc, mg_to_nmol(d), "is_subcutaneous", fig8_times(d),

}))

fig8_cmp <- fig8_pub |>
  left_join(st_fig8, by = c("dose_mg", "time")) |>

fig8_late <- fig8_cmp$time >= 2500

The quadrature mean follows the solid line of every panel: within
`r round(100 * max(abs(fig8_cmp$ratio_mean[fig8_to3000] - 1)), 1)`% at all
`r sum(fig8_to3000)` points up to 3000 h. The 900 mg panel runs to
6000 h, and there the mean is
`r sprintf("%.2f", fig8_c_at(5000))` of the line at 5000 h and
`r sprintf("%.2f", fig8_c_at(5900))` at 5900 h. The median of the
200-antibody cohort is within
`r round(100 * max(abs(fig8_cmp$ratio_median[fig8_early] - 1)))`% of the
line up to 500 h but falls below it later: from 2500 h its ratio to the
line has a median of
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(fig8_cmp$ratio_median[fig8_late]))`. The
published line is therefore read as the mean.

At 600 mg the cohort's 95th percentiles are within a factor of
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(max(abs(log(fig8_p95$ratio)))))` of the published
band. Its 5th percentiles are
`r sprintf("%.2f", fig8_p05$ratio[1])`,
`r sprintf("%.2f", fig8_p05$ratio[2])` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", fig8_p05$ratio[3])` times the published ones at
`r fig8_p05$time[1]`, `r fig8_p05$time[2]` and `r fig8_p05$time[3]` h.
They point the same way as in Supplementary Figure S1, where the published
5th percentile is lower than the simulated one by a factor of
`r sprintf("%.1f", s1_p05_late[1])`-`r sprintf("%.1f", s1_p05_late[2])` from
300 h: in both figures the model's lower tail, the antibodies that
are cleared fastest, is thinner than the paper's, and more so as time
goes on. A separate simulation of 20000 antibodies, not run in this
article, puts the population 5th percentiles at 1.07, 1.14 and 1.66 times
the published values at the same three times.

At 2950 h sampling adds to that difference. The reading there,
0.006 ug/mL, is `r round(fig8_tail_decades, 1)` decades below the
published 95th percentile, and the 5th percentile of 200 antibodies at
that time changes by a factor of about ten from one cohort to another:
in the same separate simulation it ranged from 0.5 to 5.4 times the
published value (1st to 99th percentile of 200-antibody cohorts). The
reading is also a dashed line at the foot of a five-decade axis, the
least certain in the figure. That point is therefore held only to a
factor of 6 (here `r sprintf("%.1f", fig8_band_cmp$ratio[fig8_tail])`),
and the other four band readings to a factor of 2.5.

The observed profiles of the nine validation antibodies are not reproduced
here: Kumar 2024 overlays digitised data that are not tabulated in the
paper or its supplement.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **`CLup` scales by per-tissue endosomal volume.** Resolved in favour of
  the Chang 2019 printed form over the Shah & Betts ADAPT code's
  total-endosomal-volume form, because Kumar 2024's `CLup` estimate is on
  the per-tissue scale; see reconciliation 1.
* **Brain compartment retained.** Kumar 2024 Section 2.2's tissue list omits
  the brain, but Figure 1 draws it and the Section 2.5 central-volume
  arithmetic requires it (1412 mL is reproduced exactly only with the brain
  subtracted). Treated as a prose omission in the paper.
* **`S_LU` applied to the lymph-node inflow as well as the SC efflux.** The
  literal reading of the two printed equations is not mass-conserving and
  produces the wrong sign in the Figure 7 sensitivity analysis.
* **`S_LU` sensitivity is ~1.5x the published magnitude.** The `kSC` arm of
  Figure 7 matches exactly, which isolates the discrepancy to how mAb
  escapes the SC site. The most likely contributors are the SC
  sub-compartment volumes in Table 1, which are printed to one or two
  significant figures (the endosomal volume is given as "0.03" mL, where
  preserving the skin sub-compartment ratios the paper describes gives
  0.034 mL), and the SC lymph flow, which the paper says was "scaled down"
  but never tabulates - it is taken here as plasma flow / 500, the Shah &
  Betts rule. No parameter was adjusted to close the gap.
* **Figure 8's solid line is compared with the mean over the antibody
  population.** The caption does not name the statistic. The mean, computed
  by Gauss-Hermite quadrature over the four random effects, reproduces all
  nine panels within
  `r round(100 * max(abs(fig8_cmp$ratio_mean[fig8_to3000] - 1)), 1)`% up to
  3000 h, while the median of a 200-antibody cohort falls below it: from
  2500 h its ratio to the line has a median of
  `r sprintf("%.2f", median(fig8_cmp$ratio_median[fig8_late]))`.
* **After about 200 h the published IV median declines faster than this
  model.** In Supplementary Figure S1 (1 mg/kg IV) the median of 200
  simulated antibodies is within
  `r round(100 * max(abs(s1_cmp$ratio[s1_early] - 1)), 1)`% of the
  published one over 42-150 h but
  `r round(100 * (s1_ratio_at(690) - 1))`% above it at 690 h (half-life over
  300-690 h: `r round(s1_thalf(s1_cmp$published), 1)` days published,
  `r round(s1_thalf(s1_cmp$simulated), 1)` days simulated), and the
  published 5th percentile is lower, by a factor of up to
  `r round(max(s1_lo$ratio), 1)`. The cause was not determined. The form of
  the pinocytosis clearance does not explain it: with the whole-body form
  the median is
  `r round(100 * min(s1_wb_below))`-`r round(100 * max(s1_wb_below))`%
  below the published one over 42-150 h, where the packaged model matches
  it. The SC window of Figure 8, which rests on the same disposition model,
  is reproduced up to 3000 h.
* **`omega` values read as log-scale standard deviations.** The paper
  reports `omega_CLup` = 73%, `omega_kdeg` = 46%, `omega_kSC` = 193%,
  `omega_S_LU` = 49% without stating whether these are SDs of the random
  effect or CV%. They are encoded as SDs (the Monolix native output and the
  usual reading of `omega`), so `ini()` carries the squares. The empirical
  spread of the individual estimates in Kumar 2024 Figure 6 is consistent
  with this reading; a CV% reading would give `omega_CLup` = 0.65 rather
  than 0.73, a modest narrowing of the prediction window.
* **Random effects are inter-ANTIBODY, not between-subject.** Each antibody
  was treated as an individual during fitting. Simulating with the etas
  active generates a range of plausible antibody-level typical profiles,
  which is exactly the paper's intended use (the Figure 8 prediction
  window). It does **not** describe patient-to-patient variability for a
  single antibody, and these models should not be used to size a study.
* **No residual error model.** Kumar 2024 specified a combined error model
  in Monolix but does not report its coefficients anywhere in the paper or
  supplement, so no `propSd` / `addSd` is included. Both files are
  typical-value plus inter-antibody simulators.
* **Lung plasma flow derived for mass-balance closure.** The Table 4 lung
  flows equal the sums of the tissue flows plus the "Ly. Node" row: 181.913
  L/h of plasma against the 178.244 L/h the tissues take in, about 2% more.
  Used literally, they remove mAb at the lung outflow. `q_lu` is derived as
  `sum(q_X) / (1 - 1/500)` and `bcq_lu` as `sum(bcq_X)`.
* **`C_LNLF` not carried.** Kumar 2024 inherits Shah & Betts' `C_LNLF`
  = 9.1. The Shah & Betts ADAPT code and Chang 2019 set the lymph-node
  outflow to `C_LNLF` times the lung plasma flow; this model uses the
  Table 4 "Ly. Node" flow (3.670 L/h) instead, so `C_LNLF` does not enter
  the ODEs and is omitted from `ini()`. Plasma concentrations hardly depend
  on this outflow (in the `Shah_2012_mAb_PBPK` vignette the two choices
  differ by under 0.1%).
* **No antigen binding, no TMDD.** By construction: antibodies with
  nonlinear PK were excluded from the dataset.
* **Approval status is documented, not modelled.** Kumar 2024 compares the
  individual parameter distributions of FDA-approved versus clinically
  tested mAbs (Figure 6) and reports the medians, but concludes there is no
  clear distinction and never enters approval status into the model. It is
  recorded in `covariatesDataExcluded` for provenance.
